notes.trap: `length(...)` counts characters, not bytes, and trailing spaces are counted. SQL Server's LEN ignores trailing spaces; Spark does not. Use `octet_length(...)` for the byte count.
Returns the UTF-8 byte count of a string, which differs from `length(...)` for any non-ASCII character.
When the optional threshold argument is given and the distance exceeds it, the result is -1, not NULL and not the threshold. Comparison is case-sensitive.
Argument order is (substr, str), the reverse of `instr(...)`. A start position below 1 returns 0 rather than searching from the beginning. A NULL start position also returns 0, not NULL.

The function form is position(substr, str), the reverse of `instr(str, substr)`. Swapping the arguments silently searches for the wrong thing and usually returns 0. The SQL-standard form is POSITION(substr IN str).

If the string is already longer than len, `lpad(...)` truncates it to len characters, keeping the leftmost characters. It does not return the string unchanged and does not keep the rightmost characters.
An empty pad string performs no padding, so the input comes back unchanged and shorter than len. A len shorter than the input truncates it.
The one-argument form removes only the space character (0x20). Tabs, newlines and other whitespace are kept.
Any non-digit character, including the dashes or spaces common in formatted card numbers, makes the result false. It does not raise an error and does not ignore those characters.
By default only letters and digits are masked; otherChar defaults to NULL, so spaces and punctuation are kept as-is. Digits become 'n', not 'X'.
When FOR len is omitted, the number of characters replaced equals the length of the replacement string, not the rest of the input.
A NULL argument does not make the result NULL. Java's formatter prints it as the text 'null'.
Counts non-overlapping matches only. After a match, scanning resumes after the end of that match.
When nothing matches, the result is an empty string, not NULL. The default idx is 1, so a pattern with no capture group fails unless you pass idx 0.
The default idx is 1, so the pattern needs a capture group, otherwise pass 0. No match yields an empty array rather than NULL.
The replacement string uses Java regex syntax: $1, $2 refer to capture groups. A literal dollar sign or backslash in rep must be escaped.
Unlike `regexp_extract(...)`, which returns an empty string on no match, `regexp_substr(...)` returns NULL when the pattern is not found.
A zero or negative count returns an empty string rather than NULL or an error.
`replace(...)` matches search literally (no regex) and case-sensitively. With only two arguments it deletes every occurrence of search.
